newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan drops opposition to Russian entry to G7.
newsitem.headline: Japan drops opposition to Russian entry to G7.

text.p: Japan has reversed its position and agreed to let Russia join the Denver summit of the world's leading industrialised nations next month as a formal member, Kyodo news agency quoted government sources as saying on Sunday.
The Japanese government decided to reverse its stance on the June 20-22 summit talks because the other Group of Seven (G7) members were in favour of admitting Russia, the report said.
"It would not be a wise policy for Japan alone to voice caution," Kyodo quoted a senior foreign ministry official as saying.

Japan will convey its approval at the meeting of summit "sherpas" to be held later this month in the United States, when officials will prepare for the summit. Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda was also expected to relay Japan's support when he visits Russia on Thursday, Kyodo said.

The G7 members are Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. President Bill Clinton said at a summit with Russia's Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki in March that the Group would grant Russia a bigger role and turn its annual meeting into a "Summit of the Eight".

The Kyodo report came as Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov wrapped up a visit to Japan in which he promised troop cuts and expanded defence exchanges with Tokyo and gave Moscow's blessing to closer U.S.-Japan military ties.

The Soviet Union first joined the annual G7 summit meetings in London in 1991 when then President Mikhail Gorbachev held talks with G7 leaders. After the Soviet Union's collapse, Russian President Boris Yeltsin took part in summits as an observer.

Behind Japan's reluctance to have Russia as a formal member is a territorial dispute over four islands off Japan's northernmost main island of Hokkaido which the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War Two.
